1:1: The prophecy of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord God to Edom – A report have we heard from before the Lord and a messenger into the nations has he sent. Arise and let us prepare ourselves for battle against her.
1:2: Behold, I will make you weak among the nations. You are highly contemptible.
1:3: The wickedness of your heart has led you astray. For you are like an eagle that dwells in the teeth of the rock, whose dwelling-place is in the heights, who says in his heart, “Who will bring me down to earth?”
1:4: If you soar like an eagle and if you set your abode between the stars, from there I will bring you down, saith the Lord.
1:5: If thieves came upon you, if plunderers of the night – How then would you sleep until they had stolen their fill! And if robbers, as grape-cutters, came upon you – Would they not leave gleanings?
1:6: How then has Esau been ransacked! His hidden things have been revealed.
1:7: You have been driven from the border. All the men of your covenant have led you astray. Those who were at peace with you have prevailed against you. Those who eat your bread have set a snare underneath you, because you lacked sense.
1:8: Shall I not in that era, saith the Lord, destroy the wise men of Edom and any man who has sense from the city of Esau?
1:9: And your warriors who dwell in the south shall be smashed, in order to destroy any man with the mark of the City of Esau, through slaughter.
1:10: For violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered in disgrace and you will be destroyed forever.
1:11: On the day you stood aside, on the day the nations plundered his possessions and strangers entered his forts and cast lots upon Jerusalem, even you were like one of them.
1:12: And that you watched on the day of your brother on the day of his destruction, and that you rejoiced over the children of Judah on the day of their destruction, and that you went on to speak boastfully in a time of trouble.
1:13: And that you entered the gates of my nation on the day of their destruction, and that even you watched his affliction of the day of his destruction, and that you laid your hand on his possessions on the day of his destruction.
1:14: And that you stood on the cross-road to cut off his refugees and that you handed over his survivors in a time of trouble.
1:15: Because the day is near, that will come before the Lord, upon all nations. What you have done will be done to you. Your deeds will be returned to your head.
1:16: For just as you rejoiced over the smiting of my holy mountain, so will all the nations drink constantly from the cup of their punishment. And they shall drink and be confounded and they shall be as if they never existed.
1:17: And in Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and they will be holy. And the House of Jacob shall inherit the possessions of the nations who had inherited from them.
1:18: And the House of Jacob shall be mighty as fire and the House of Joseph as strong as flame and the House of Esau as weak as straw. And they shall dominate them and kill them and there will no survivor for the House of Esau, for the Lord has decreed it so.
1:19: And those who dwell in the south shall inherit the City of Esau. And those who dwell in the plains (shall inherit) the lands of the Philistines and they shall inherit the villages of Ephraim and the villages of Samaria. And the house of Benjamin (shall inherit) those who dwell in the land of Gilead.
1:20: And the exiles of this nation of the Children of Israel that is in the land of the Canaanites (shall inherit) until Zerapahath. And the exiles of Jerusalem that are in Ispamiah will inherit the villages of the south land.
1:21: And saviors shall ascend Mount Zion to judge the City of Esau and the Kingdom of the Lord shall be revealed upon all inhabitants of the earth.

n: T

- The word *vision* introduces a prophetic book ({{Isaiah 1:1|Isaiah 1:1}}; {{Nahum 1:1|Nahum 1:1}}). It also describes what a prophet saw or sensed as a divine message ({{Ezekiel 12:26-27|Ezekiel 12:26–27}}; {{Daniel 8:1|Daniel 8:1}}). A vision not from the Lord was false ({{Jeremiah 14:14|Jeremiah 14:14}}; {{Jeremiah 23:16|23:16}}), proven by its failure to happen ({{Ezekiel 12:22-24|Ezekiel 12:22–24}}). In contrast, true visions of events, whether near or far, do happen ({{Ezekiel 12:25|Ezekiel 12:25}}; {{Habakkuk 2:3|Habakkuk 2:3}}). Prophetic visions appeared in different forms, like dreams or extrasensory experiences (for example, {{Daniel 8:2|Daniel 8:2}}). The lack of visions shows divine abandonment ({{Lamentations 2:9|Lamentations 2:9}}; {{Ezekiel 7:26|Ezekiel 7:26}}; {{Micah 3:6|Micah 3:6}}). 

- Obadiah was a common Hebrew name meaning “servant of the Lord.” The prophet Obadiah is unknown outside this book. 

- *an envoy has been sent among the nations*: In ancient warfare, allies were contacted to join a military group to punish an enemy or defend against an attack. Here, the Sovereign Lord calls the nations to address Edom’s evil pride. 

- *let us god to battle*: This is a willing group, but ironically, they will later be punished for their own evil actions ({{Obadiah 15-16|Obadiah 1:15–16}}).
B

The prophet Obadiah announced messages of judgement against Edom. These were like the messages of judgement against Edom recorded in Jeremiah 49. Obadiah explained why God would bring judgement against Edom. The Edomites were proud. They believed that their strength and wisdom kept them safe. This showed that they didn’t respect God’s authority as the Lord and King. Their pride also showed that they didn’t respect God’s authority over the people of Judah.

God chose to make a covenant with the people from the family line of Jacob. The Edomites were their relatives. Yet people from Esau’s and Jacob’s family lines didn’t live in peace with one another. That had been the case for hundreds of years. The Edomites made it clear that they didn’t respect God or his choices. They made this clear when Jerusalem was attacked.

God allowed Jerusalem to be destroyed by Babylonian armies in 586 BC. That was how God brought judgement against the southern kingdom. The Edomites didn’t respect that God was taking action against his people (God’s people). Instead they took action and made the suffering of the southern kingdom worse. Obadiah explained many evil things that the Edomites did to the people of the southern kingdom. Other parts of the Bible show how the people of Jerusalem felt about that. Psalm 137 and Lamentations chapters 2 and 4 are examples.

Obadiah announced that God would destroy the Edomites because of their pride and evil deeds. Obadiah described that time of judgement as the day of the Lord. It was a time when God would judge not only Edom but also all nations. Obadiah described God’s anger like a cup that the nations would drink from. The result of the judgement against the nations would be blessing for God’s people. They would enjoy the covenant blessings. This included living safely in the land God had promised to Abraham’s family line. It included the blessing of God’s presence. That is what was meant by Zion being the holy mountain once again. God described this time of blessing as a kingdom that belonged to him.

Jews came to understand this message of hope as a prophecy for the future. It would be fulfilled when God sent the messiah. New Testament writers came to understand that Jesus is the Messiah. Jesus announced that he brought the kingdom of God to earth.
T

- *I will make you small*: Several messages of judgment describe Edom’s specific sins against Israel ({{Obadiah 10-14|Obadiah 1:10–14}}; {{Jeremiah 49:7-22|Jeremiah 49:7–22}}; {{Ezekiel 25:12-14|Ezekiel 25:12–14}}; {{Ezekiel 36:5|36:5}}). Edom often appears among the nations that opposed Israel and the Lord ({{Isaiah 34:1-17|Isaiah 34}}; {{Ezekiel 35:1-36:38|Ezekiel 35–36}}; {{Amos 9:1-15|Amos 9:1–15}}). 

- *small among the nations … The pride of your heart*: Edom’s rocky landscape reflected the pride of its people. Just as their land was high and difficult to reach, the people of Edom thought they were secure and above others. The height of the mountain fortress that provided their security only highlights the height from which Edom would fall. Edomite princes were among the arrogant rulers of the nations ({{Ezekiel 32:29|Ezekiel 32:29}}; compare {{Genesis 36:1-43|Genesis 36}}; {{1 Chronicles 1:43-54|1 Chronicles 1:43–54}}).
T

Edom's destroyers would take everything, unlike thieves and harvesters. Thieves would leave anything that might slow their escape. Harvesters would always leave some leftovers for the poor ({{Deuteronomy 24:19|Deuteronomy 24:19}}; compare {{Ruth 2:1-23|Ruth 2}}; {{Matthew 12:1|Matthew 12:1}}).
T
The Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem completely. Edom shared in the loot, so they deserved the same punishment (see {{Obadiah 15-18|Obadiah 1:15–18}}).
T
*Esau*: The Hebrew text uses the name of Esau, who was Jacob’s brother. This shows Edom broke a brotherly relationship ({{Obadiah 10-14|Obadiah 1:10–14}}).
T

- *men allied with you *(literally *men of the covenant*): Edom should have been Israel's ally, but instead, Edom made a covenant with Babylon. 

- *men of peace* (paralleling *men of the covenant*): This was a fitting form of justice. Edom betrayed Israel, and later, Babylon betrayed Edom in the same way.
T

- *In that day*: The Hebrew word *yom*, meaning “day,” appears 12 times in {{Obadiah 8-15|Obadiah 1:8–15}}. It is often translated as “when” or “at that time.” The time mentioned in {{Obadiah 8|Obadiah 1:8}} marks the start of the end, when God intervenes to change the fate of his people. 

- *wise men … men of understanding*: Edom was proud of its wisdom tradition (see {{Jeremiah 49:7|Jeremiah 49:7}}). For instance, the book of Job takes place in Edomite land.
T

*Because of the violence against your brother Jacob*: The reason for Esau’s condemnation is explained in {{Obadiah 10|Obadiah 1:10}} (see also {{Isaiah 34:1-17|Isaiah 34}}; {{Jeremiah 49:7-22|Jeremiah 49:7–22}}; {{Joel 3:19|Joel 3:19}}; {{Amos 1:11-12|Amos 1:11–12}}) and expanded in {{Obadiah 11-14|Obadiah 1:11–14}}, where Edom’s betrayal is described. In legal terms, these verses provide evidence for the charge of breaking a covenant.
T

Outside of this book, we know little about Edom's role during the Babylonian invasions of Judah in 605, 597, and 586 BC. God's law requires responsibility toward one's neighbor (for example, {{Deuteronomy 22:1-4|Deuteronomy 22:1–4}}; compare {{Matthew 25:41-46|Matthew 25:41–46}}), especially when there is a specific *covenant of brotherhood* ({{Amos 1:9|Amos 1:9}}) or a historical relationship which biblical writers considered a relationship between brothers (see study note on Obadiah 1:6).
T

- The tribes of Israel were relatives of Edom (literally *brother;* compare {{Numbers 20:14|Numbers 20:14}}). 

- Edom and other nearby nations mistakenly believed that making peace with Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC would give them relief. However, their time of judgment would come.
T

All societies are responsible for wrongdoings, like those of Edom (see, for example, the messages against Israel’s neighbors in {{Amos 1:3-2:3|Amos 1:3–2:3}}). The Edomites committed sins against Judah by helping the Babylonians loot the land ({{Obadiah 13|Obadiah 1:13}}) and either killing or sending back Judah’s escapees ({{Obadiah 14|1:14}}).
T

- *The Day of the LORD is near*: The phrase *the day of the Lord* sometimes referred to a specific event, like the destruction of Edom or Joel’s locust plague ({{Joel 1:15|Joel 1:15}}). In its final form, it represents God's final judgment on all godless nations. 

- *As you have done*: Those who face judgment will find their punishment reflects their evil actions.
T

The law of retribution (*lex talionis*) means we face the consequences of our actions. Edom's betrayal and pride would lead to her own downfall when vengeance came. Justice would deliver Israel and punish Edom (see also {{Jeremiah 49:7-22|Jeremiah 49:7–22}}; {{Ezekiel 32:29|Ezekiel 32:29}}; {{Malachi 1:2-5|Malachi 1:2–5}}).
T

- Jerusalem would become a safe place for those who escape. A small group from Judah stayed in Jerusalem (see {{Jeremiah 40:11-12|Jeremiah 40:11–12}}). The Lord’s mountain of refuge stands in stark contrast to Edom’s failed cliff fortresses. 

- *their possession*: The land God gave to Abraham ({{Genesis 12:1-7|Genesis 12:1–7}}) would be returned to his descendants forever. 

- *the house of Jacob*: The prophet Malachi mentioned the promise of return for the people of Judah, but not for the Edomites ({{Malachi 1:4-5|Malachi 1:4–5}}).
T
The idea of retribution is shown through the image of a fierce fire destroying Edom completely. Babylonian King Nabonidus burned Edomite cities in 553 BC.
T

God's people in the Negev, the foothills of Judah, and Benjamin (three regions of Judah) would take over their neighbors' territories (Edom, the Philistine plains, Gilead). Restored Israel would regain Ephraim and Samaria (territory lost from 722 to 721 BC to Assyria) and expand its borders to the lands promised during the conquest (the Philistine plains, the land of Gilead, the Phoenician coast). See also {{Ezekiel 47:13-23|Ezekiel 47:13–23}}.
T
History moves toward a day when the Lord will rule over the whole world as his kingdom. This message gives hope to God’s people and warns the nations that ignore him.
T
*in Sepharad*: This likely refers to a group of Jewish exiles in Asia Minor. They would return to the Negev. The scene matches some real events but also looks forward to the end times.
T
*Mount Zion*: God's people would climb his holy mountain to rule over (or *to judge*) the mountains of their ancient enemy Edom. This would be a sign of the coming universal kingdom.
